Polarity. An uneven share of electrons gives a molecule two charged ends.
Hydrogen bonding. The + H of one water molecule attracts the − O of another.
Solvation. Water is polar, so it dissolves anything polar or charged.
Ice & density. Unlike almost every substance, water is less dense as a solid.
Heat & temperature. Water takes a lot of heating, because the energy goes into breaking H-bonds first.
Cohesion & adhesion. Water sticks to itself and to other things.
The hydrophobic effect. Oil and water separate because the water gains freedom by it.
Dehydration & hydrolysis. Monomers join by losing a water, and water splits them apart again.
Entropy. Order can rise in one place as long as more disorder is made somewhere else.
Acids & pH. A buffer trades protons back and forth, so pH barely moves.
Base pairing. A pairs only with T and G only with C, because that is where the hydrogen bonds line up.
Replication & fidelity. Copying is proofread as it goes, and the error rate is low but never zero.
Binding & recognition. Two molecules stick because their shapes and charges match, and neither is changed by it.
Enzyme catalysis. An enzyme lowers the barrier and comes out the other side unchanged.
Levels of structure. A protein has four levels of structure, and the sequence decides all four.
Cooperativity. One oxygen binding changes the shape, and makes the next one easier.
Channels & pumps. A channel lets things through; a pump spends ATP to push them the wrong way.
Monomers & polymers. Four classes of macromolecule, each one a chain of repeating units.
Glycolysis. Ten steps split one sugar in two, spending two ATP to make four.
The Krebs cycle. Eight steps take two carbons off as CO₂ and hand the electrons to NADH, rebuilding the molecule they started from.
Chemiosmosis. Food pays to pump protons out of the mitochondrion; they fall back in through a rotary motor, and that fall is what makes the ATP.
Molecular geometry. Electron pairs push each other apart, and that is what sets the shape.
Covalent bonding. Two atoms share a pair of electrons, and both count them as their own.
Ionic bonding. One atom takes the electron outright, and the two ions hold on by charge.
Osmosis. Water crosses toward the saltier side with nothing pushing it.
The bilayer. Phospholipids assemble into a sheet on their own, because their tails avoid water.
Denaturing. Heat and acid unfold a protein without breaking a single covalent bond.
Folding. The chain folds to one shape out of astronomically many, and the sequence picks it.
Simple diffusion. Random motion spreads molecules out; going twice as far takes four times as long.
